subsubtopic: PROPOSED TASK FORCE TO DETERMINE MEASURES TO AID SYDNEY STEEL OPERATION-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 43, I seek the unanimous consent of the House to propose a motion on a matter of urgent, pressing and grave necessity.
In view of the extremely high level of unemployment in the Cape Breton area of Nova Scotia which has been aggravated by a series of layoffs at the Sysco steel operations at Sydney, amounting to over 800 employees, which will in all probability be followed by additional layoffs as a result of a massive breakdown in the rail mill, coupled with the fact that cheap foreign reinforcing steel is entering Nova Scotia while Sysco has a stockpile of such material, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Cumber-land-Colchester North (Mr. Coates):
That the Department of Regional Economic Expansion combine with the Departments of Labour and Manpower and Immigration to form a task force of experts from these departments to immediately go to Sydney to determine what urgent actions can be initiated, both technically and financially, to overcome the terrible economic crisis that has beset the total community and the impending possible collapse of the present operation, with no concrete indication by the federal and provincial governments that Cape Breton Island will definitely be the site of the proposed and promised new steel complex.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 43, I seek the unanimous consent of the House to move a motion on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
Considering that $4 billion will be paid out during 1975-76 in unemployment insurance benefits, that this money will serve to support people doing nothing, while a mere $150 million will be used to create jobs under the LIP program, taking into account the great advertising campaign on the radio to invite people to submit projects, and the fact that a great many projects may be turned down for lack of funds, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Kamouraska (Mr. Dionne):

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I read a report in the Globe and Mail this morning about the meeting I had yesterday with the Ontario ministers and I think it contains only one inaccuracy. The cabinet asked me to report on the meeting, and that is all, but if I read the Globe and Mail article correctly, it states that a new decision is supposed to be made about Pickering airport. This is not what the cabinet asked me to do. I was just asked by the cabinet to make a report.

It is even worse than I had expected.
That is impossible.

In view of the uncertainty, not only for the people in Ontario as a whole, but in particular for the people who live in the municipalities directly affected by the Pickering airport decision in terms of the zoning plans for the years ahead, can the minister tell us now what the government's intention is because of the new uncertainty that had arisen about building up until 1977, and then what precisely does he plan to do beyond 1977? Does he have a full scale airport in mind beyond 1977?

If the
hon. gentleman read the whole article he would have seen that I will recommend to cabinet that we stick to our decision and that nothing be changed.
Hear, hear!

Of course, cabinet has the authority to change the whole thing. This is the Government of Canada and they can say no. But this will not be my recommendation. My recommendation is to the effect that we should stick to the decision we made to construct first a mini-airport to be completed by 1977, and only then will we decide whether we want to go all the way.

We will not be entirely surprised if the cabinet does change its mind. But if the minister is saying to the House that in 1977 the government will make another decision on what will happen beyond 1977, I would like to ask him what he meant in his letter to Premier Davis dated June 12 and tabled in the Ontario legislature on July 11, when he said that federal plans were proceeding for a "subsequent phase of development for Pickering for implementation by 1981". The implication is that the plans are already made for beyond 1977. Elsewhere in the letter the clear indication is of a full scale airport. If so, can the minister tell the House now whether that is the federal government's intention now?

What I have said to the
House and in public still holds true. This means that we
Oral Questions
will build a mini-airport with one runway and a terminal, of course, and in 1977, if new facts come up, we will reassess the situation because technology in that field can bring something new and perhaps Canadians might feel that the time has come for the situation to be reassessed. However, our decision is to build a completely new airport in Pickering with the proviso that in 1977 there will be a reassessment in case new facts are brought to light.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on July 18 I addressed the following question to the Minister of the Environment and the Minister of Fisheries, as reported at page 7704 of Hansard:
In view of the tender call for the charter of two vessels by the federal fisheries and marine service for exploratory fishing for swordfish during the months of July and August, could the minister indicate the reason for this exploratory work and inform the House if the United States food and drug directorate has lifted the import ban on swordfish as imposed some four years ago?
She promised to take that question up with the Minister of State (Fisheries), and since he is in the House today could he provide me with an answer, for many fishermen in Nova Scotia are eagerly awaiting the minister's report.

subtopic: REASON FOR EXPLORATORY FISHING FOR SWORDFISH-POSSIBLE LIFTING OF IMPORT BAN ON SWORDFISH BY UNITED STATES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as indicated, the program involving these two ships is very much intended to be experimental. One is to check again the mercury content and certain age levels of swordfish and also, although we are not very hopeful, we are trying to explore the possibility of removing mercury from the flesh. There is really nothing much more than that; it is strictly experimental.

subtopic: REASON FOR EXPLORATORY FISHING FOR SWORDFISH-POSSIBLE LIFTING OF IMPORT BAN ON SWORDFISH BY UNITED STATES
speechtext: A brief supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. In light of the fact that there are ships at the present time from other countries fishing for swordfish off the coast of Nova Scotia, would the minister indicate where these ships are finding a market for swordfish?

subtopic: REASON FOR EXPLORATORY FISHING FOR SWORDFISH-POSSIBLE LIFTING OF IMPORT BAN ON SWORDFISH BY UNITED STATES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, some nations do not seem to mind the mercury content of swordfish at the moment and do use it. We have no prohibition against selling fish if anyone wants to buy it. The problem is to find a market. Some states of the United States-this is a state matter-do allow consumption and selling within the state of swordfish products. We have a prohibition against it here in Canada, because of mercury levels, and there is no way we can export swordfish through the normal avenues if the U.S. government has banned imports.

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subsubtopic: REASON FOR SHORTAGE OF HOME CANNING MATERIALS- GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the problem exists not only in Canada but also in the United States. Several months ago, we took steps to help the Canadian companies. The Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce made sure that the two Canadian companies would have enough tin plate to meet the demand. Officials of my department visited those companies to encourage them to produce more of it, to double and even triple their production, which they did. Unfortunately, there was a shortage of the product in some sectors, but I can assure the hon. member that as far as the Canadian companies are concerned, they are producing at full capacity. We can do no more. Attempts will therefore have to be made to import some to make up the shortage. This is becoming increasingly difficult, as a similar shortage exists in the United States. Canadian consumers will therefore be asked to buy only what they need, and refrain from hoarding it for fear the shortage might become even more acute.

Order, please. I have the greatest respect for the rights of the hon. member who has just raised this question, as well as of other hon. members, to function freely without interference. The letter the hon. member has put forward, on the face of it at least, seems to me to be no more than correspondence with the hon. member containing an invitation or a suggestion. It may go further, but if the hon. member has any disagreement in that regard he may want to take this up as a matter of discussion with the minister or other officials of his department, other ministers, or the Prime Minister.
However, in order to fall within the category of a question of privilege there would have to be some indication of a step taken which in fact constituted a direct interference with the right of the hon. member to function as a member of parliament. In fact what this seems to be is correspondence about a suggestion of the member, indicating it ought to be discussed further.
The hon. member's right to speak in this House, to function as a member, and to make suggestions has certainly not been restrained or interfered with, but what reception is given might be a matter of disagreement by the hon. member, as it has been by several other members. With all due respect to the hon. member, I do not think this is the right forum or the right guise, under the title of a question of privilege, to get into a debate as to whether the list contained proper and adequate representation of his own constituency or the texture of it at this time. Unless the member is able to show there has been in fact a restriction or hindrance of his right to function as a member, to make suggestions, and to have a part in the decision-making process, I would have to indicate that there is no question of privilege.
Mr. Speaker, perhaps I might be permitted to continue. This did not begin just this month. Last fall when I submitted a similar list I got the same response, only it was verbal.
Oh, oh!
Not only did it come from the minister's office, the Moncton Liberal Association laid a complaint in the local newspaper, unfounded. I am concerned that there is political patronage here.
Oh, oh!
Now he will be called to order.
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order, please. The hon. member for Cumberland-Colchester North will have sensed that I had initially rejected the representations of the hon. member for Moncton as a question of privilege, unless there was some clear and distinct interference with his rights. The minister made a comment on this and I did not think it needed a further decision on my part to indicate that, in the final analysis, the hon. member for Moncton was not putting a motion in respect of the proposed question of privilege.
Furthermore, I had some difficulty in that the minister was on his feet prior to that point, and I went back to him by way of recognition. If the hon. member for Cumberland-Colchester North wants to contribute before I do finalize the question put by the hon. member for Moncton, I would be glad to see him now.

Mr. Speaker, probably I would not have intervened in this debate except for the fact that, after you had ruled, the Minister of Justice got up and put in his two cents, which is just exactly what his comments are worth, as far as I am concerned.
There is no question but that the rights of a member of parliament in this House are being interfered with when the Minister of Manpower and Immigration writes a letter

requesting that a member place before him a list containing certain people within the constituency he has been elected to represent by the majority of the people. Whether the people in government authority do or do not like the way he was elected, the member is still here because he represents his constituency, having been elected by a majority of the people.
In this case the minister has written the hon. member requesting the member to provide a list of nominees in his constituency he feels would assist the Minister of Manpower and Immigration and the people involved with the Local Initiatives Program to produce recommendations, which are not final in any way, in order that the minister and these people in the Local Initiatives Program can make a decision on which projects should be undertaken in that constituency. Following that, in this case some executive assistant, special assistant or somebody else in that department, had the unmitigated gall to write the hon. member saying in effect that he did not like the way the member had made up the list of people, which in the first place he was asked to provide. I think this is getting to be a bit too much. I think it is a rank interference with the rights and privileges of a member of parliament, and I think that you, Sir, should provide some protection.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order, please. If there are no other hon. members who wish to speak to the matter, let me make the situation perfectly clear. The hon. member for Moncton has raised a grievance about the administration of a program, and about whether a decision of that sort ought to be handled by the minister or through representations by any hon. member of the House. That may in fact be a legitimate criticism or grievance on the part of the hon. member.
What I am concerned with here is not whether there is a disagreement about the administration of a program of this nature, the texture of the program, or the manner in which the minister deals with members in receiving representations. What I am concerned with here is whether this in fact constitutes a question of privilege within the very narrow confines of the rules of this House, which have recognized in the past, and I think quite rightly so, that only specialized classes of problems come within the confines of a question of privilege. I find that this matter does not. In any case, no motion has been put forward suggesting action by the Chair. Again I say that what may be a very legitimate grievance can be taken up in a number of ways.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order because of the question of the hon. member for St. John's East. I do not want to leave the impression with the House-and I hope he was not suggesting either-that the Farm Products Marketing Council was acting beyond the jurisdiction vested in it by the legislation. The person on the board he mentioned says she is optimistic about the new job she is taking on and that there will be public hearings, and so on. She is not as pessimistic as the hon. member tries to make out she is.

Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to take up much time of the House with my question of privilege of
July 30, 1975

which I have given you notice. It arose out of the question yesterday which I submitted was perfectly proper in the light of what happened in the city of Hamilton. I think it was very pertinent.
My question of privilege relates to an exchange in the House yesterday, as Your Honour is well aware, between myself and the Minister of Labour, as recorded in Hansard at pages 8021 and 8026. During that exchange the minister made some rather serious accusations about myself which I feel I cannot let go unanswered, and which I believe constitute a legitimate question of privilege. Specifically, Mr. Speaker, as recorded at page 8026 of Hansard, the minister accused me of "indecency in casting innuendoes" and of what he terms "disgraceful conduct". Those are serious charges and ones for which I am entitled, I submit, to receive rather more specific allegations or a retraction from the minister.
The minister made these imputations against me in specific reference to questions which were raised during this session by myself and others in respect of the status of two federal appointees to the Hamilton Harbour Commission-Messrs. Lanza and Hickey. I have reviewed the issues of Hansard on this matter and I have no hesitation, Mr. Speaker, in challenging the Minister of Labour as I did yesterday to produce one reference to back up the kind of McCarthy-like charges he made against me yesterday.
At the same time, Mr. Speaker, I would suggest to the Minister of Labour, and I feel compelled to do this, that if he feels aggrieved in this matter over statements made against Messrs. Lanza and Hickey, he might direct his action against the Minister of Transport, for the most serious or damning statements about these gentlemen came not from this side of the House but from the Minister of Transport. I would refer the Minister of Labour in particular to page 3622 of Hansard for February 27, 1975, and this statement by his colleague, the Minister of Transport:
At that time-
The minister was referring to the time at which he declined to reappoint Messrs. Lanza and Hickey to the Commission.
-no trial had taken place-there had been no inquiry but there was suspicion and, since those jobs are given at the discretion of cabinet, nothing binds us to nominating someone who might be suspected of not, say, meeting some ethical standards .. .
Those references to suspicions about ethical standards are not mine; they are those of the Minister of Transport.
In summary, Mr. Speaker, I believe it is in order for me to raise as a matter of privilege the completely unfounded charges which the Minister of Labour made yesterday against my personal conduct as a member of this House. That was untrue, unkind, and uncalled for, and I believe it might even have been rude. I demand that the minister either make a specific charge against me or withdraw his own version of McCarthyism from the record.
Upon his failure to do so-and I hope the hon. gentleman will do this-I would move that the remarks of the hon. member contained at page 8026 of Hansard for July 29, 1975, be referred to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections for consideration and report back to the House in due course.
Privilege-Mr. MacKay
Hear, hear!

Well, Mr. Speaker, I have no intention of withdrawing my remarks. In the first place I do not feel you will find too many citations in Beau-chesne which would indicate that remarks of that nature require withdrawal. It was an opinion of mine expressed in this House about the conduct of the member, which I think is fully fortified and justified if one looks at Hansard.
The fact of the matter is that while a trial was in process the hon. member endeavoured, in a McCarthy-like fashion, to raise matters which were going on while the trial was in process. It does not take many learned or fair people in this House, or among the general public, to indicate just how unfair that is.
Of course the reason that no serious objection was taken at the time the hon. member did what I consider to be a deplorable act was that, knowing the manner and the conduct the hon. member resorted to in this particular instance, he probably would have gone right outside to the television cameras and called "cover-up". So I resisted raising that particular area. If the hon. member was serious in raising questions yesterday about the harbour matter and was not interested really in a partisan attack, raising all sorts of innuendoes, he might be prepared to justify to this House why he raised extraneous matters such as the SIU and allegations about reticence to hold inquiries. I think that extraneous matter certainly belies the good intent of the hon. member as expressed today.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order, please. The exchange yesterday between the hon. member for Central Nova and the Minister of Labour, both in the question period and in what I indicated yesterday was a non-point of order and simply an expansion of their disagreement during the question period, has today expanded into a proposed question of privilege. I think hon. members will agree that it simply is a further development of the basic disagreement between them.
The only question which remains is that raised by the hon. member for Central Nova concerning the language used yesterday by the Minister of Labour, indicating that what I understood to be remarks made by the hon. member, always in the House and always recorded in Hansard, were indecent in their innuendo and disgraceful in the conduct of the hon. member. That is an opinion that has been expressed in this House openly by the minister. The hon. member for Central Nova has taken offence at this. This is the chamber for disagreements. That is a classic case of one of them. It would have to be otherwise, in my opinion, in order to found a prima facie case of privilege, namely, that the language of the Minister of Labour was unparliamentary.
In examining the precedents I am unable to find that the expressions he has used in the way he has used them are in any way unparliamentary. They simply contain and inflame the disagreement between the two hon. members. If we are to adjourn for a prolonged period later this day, or some day soon, perhaps it will be a pity, because the

subsubtopic: CBC-PURCHASES OF AMERICAN, CANADIAN AND FOREIGN FILMS
speechtext: For each year 1971 to 1974, how much money was spent by CBC in the purchase of (a) American films (b) Canadian films (c) foreign films for showing on Canadian television?

speakeroldname: Hon. James Hugh Faulkner (Secretary of State):
subsubtopic: CBC-PURCHASES OF AMERICAN, CANADIAN AND FOREIGN FILMS
speechtext:
I am
informed by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation as follows: CBC keeps an accurate inventory control of film purchased from all sources, but records have not been kept in such a way as to make it possible to extract readily and without an inordinate amount of work, time and cost the information called for in the manner requested. When rights are purchased by CBC for film from any source, payment for these rights may be made in a variety of ways: by equal monthly instalments, by payment immediately after broadcast, by payment of a percentage of the total price on first telecast, second telecast and third telecast, etc. Since the payments for the purchase of a quantity of feature films, for example, might be spread over a period of years, with a decreasing value in terms of programming and consequently a decreasing percentage in payments, the total value of the purchase agreement would not be correctly reported if its total value were deducted in one fiscal or calendar year. In addition, many packages of film contain films of foreign origin. Given the variety of methods of payment it is a very long and costly process to extract exact figures which distinguish which monies were spent on American as distinguished from other foreign film. Since 1974, however, in the case of Canadian film, a reporting system has been set up within CBC to provide information to its management on expenditures by CBC in the private sector of the Canadian film industry. The first statement to come from this system indicates that during the period January to December 1974 CBC spent in excess of $17.5 million in the private Canadian program production industry. Of this total amount about $9.75 million was spent in acquiring the right to
July 30, 1975

broadcast films produced in Canada. Over $7.5 million was spent with private industry to pay for productions, co-productions, and production services such as processing and printing, directors and producers, film editors, technicians and sound services.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
You will note, Mr. Speaker, that I rose slowly to my feet and looked over to my left on the assumption that this motion could be passed without debate, but now I have every reason to believe that that is not likely, and under those conditions I feel I should make some contribution.
I will start by saying that I suppose ordinary people outside the House will pause and wonder what it is that has driven a group of normally intelligent people back to the House today to seek their own permission to adjourn for two and a half months after the government has indicated that we have completed the tasks which in its opinion should be disposed of prior to that time. A simplistic answer might be that there are two or three members in the House who have been suffering from an unquenchable ambition not to leave here without an unuttered thought, an ambition which some of them were almost successful in achieving yesterday even though, in order to make sure that this was done, they had to repeat some of their thoughts several times to make certain none were forgotten.
Leave the Social Credit Party out of this, Jed.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
I am sure that by this afternoon the pitcher of Baucis and Philemon will be refilled and some more thoughts will come. We are waiting for those, Madam Speaker. But that is too simplistic an answer. We may have some cause for unhappiness about being here today and some measure of resentment at the circumstances which brought it about, but it is simply not good enough to attribute the cause to what I have hinted at rather generally so far.
Let us not forget that we will be back here in precisely the same position at the end of November and in December of 1975. Let us take a look at the Order Paper. We see there Bill C-2, the so called competition bill, which has been allotted two days. Then we see the citizenship bill, no doubt a bill which will evoke some considerable debate, possibly heated debate in the House.
Then there is the Agricultural Products Co-operative Marketing Act, Bill C-21, and the stabilization bill, C-41. There is no doubt that hon. members who are on the committee which travelled west will know that that bill is sure to take a substantial amount of time and that it will be debated in a substantial way. There are a number of issues which will be raised in the debate, and I think the minister who is responsible for the bill has recognized that fact by indicating publicly that having heard some of the views presented he is prepared to see some amendments made.
Then there is Bill C-52 dealing with changes in pensions and superannuation in a number of cases, there is the bankruptcy act, Bill C-60, and the Canada Shipping Act, almost a completely new code. With all the responsibilities

which the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) has taken on himself for the next few months, I wonder how he will be able to prepare himself for that.
We see on the Order Paper two income tax bills. There are changes proposed with regard to medical care and, no matter on which side of that thorny issue one may stand, one cannot evade the acceptance of the fact that it will be a very difficult and controversial debate. Then there is Bill C-69, an act to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act, two omnibus Criminal Code amendments, and Bill C-72, the Human Rights Commission bill.
Hanging over all this like a spectre is the very strong possibility that the House may be debating the very serious, controversial, and difficult problem of capital punishment, all of this in a period of time when there are six opposition days and two holidays, plus such other emergencies as may arise and need to be disposed of within that period. One does not need to be a prophet to say that under those conditions we will be approaching the possibility of a Christmas recess in exactly the same spot as the one in which we find ourselves now, and in which we have been for the last few weeks.
Under those conditions I do not think it would do any harm for the House to take a brief look at what we can do. Can we avoid this? Is this inevitable? Is this the best and only way in which the House can operate to discharge its responsibilities with respect to the individual members in their own constituencies as well as their duty to the country.
The President of the Privy Council (Mr. Sharp) may well say, and I think with some justice, that the House has eaten its way through a very large number of bills, a fair amount of legislation, and some government motions. True enough, and I do not deny the minister's right to take some pride in that. But I point out through you, Madam Speaker, that these are substantially all matters of a pedestrian and housekeeping nature. The real problems, the serious, hard, difficult and deep rooted problems which this country faces, have not been dealt with to date. Although they have been the subject of discussion in the general debates such as the Speech from the Throne debate and the budget debate, they have not been the subject of any meaningful attack by the government or, to some extent, by members of the House.
There is the question of energy-people are forgetting about it now, but nobody can deny the necessity of taking steps which have to be taken to prepare for the situation which will develop in 8, 10, 12 years, or even sooner. This is our problem. We wait until the difficulty has come upon us and until we are overwhelmed by facts, and then we act too little and too late. Nothing has been done to deal with the problem with regard to energy, the replacement of sources of energy, pricing, and so on. The minister has taken some powers under a statute, but those powers do not contain the answer.
There is the very serious question of the rule of law and order and the extent to which people in this country have become fearful of an inability to walk the streets in safety. There are several facets of this problem, but one cannot
July 30, 1975

deny that it is very serious, and many people outside this House are deeply concerned.
There is a continuing problem of unemployment and inflation, and with regard to external affairs there has not been a meaningful debate this session. This party has tried to have such debate through the use of methods such as opposition days, but I think it is shameful that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) should go to Helsinki to participate in that glittering galaxy-to be there to make proposals, which he appears to be making today; he appears to be speaking on behalf of Canada without a prior discussion here or-that there can be a situation develop here such as was the case with the PLO without there being an opportunity for this House to have a debate though even only a debate of three or four hours, completed or concluded by a decision of the House, with the question being put. Yet there has been no meaningful debate and no decision along these lines or our foreign relations.
There is the question of the rules under which we operate in this House. Perhaps the answer to the question I first posed is that there should be changes made there. I will certainly not invite an all out debate at this time on the rules and the changes which should be made. There will be an opportunity for that this fall, but I suggest to the members of this House that we cannot go on living in this fool's paradise in this House and attempt to deal meaningfully with these problems the way we have in the past.
Hear, hear!
There is bound to be disagreement as to the method.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: As my hon. friend says, it is quite probable that there will be disagreement as to the method. It depends where one sits. Speaking for myself, over the course of some years I have never hesitated to say that government should be far more free and flexible in using the weapon of closure when in its opinion as a matter of political necessity it takes the hard decision that the debate has gone on long enough.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
That places upon the opposition parties the equal responsibility of deciding to settle down and to fight strenuously and at length legislation which we think is bad or which the people of Canada, when they know about it, will object to, or when we think the people of Canada want us as their representatives to fight, resist, and try to improve legislation. That is a political decision which the opposition has to take, and having taken that decision-and it is a decision which should not be taken lightly but should be taken in the light of all the facts and circumstances of the issues involved and in light of the time-then the opposition digs its heels in and resists to the last moment, and the onus then falls upon the government. Personally speaking, I would have no hesitation in seeing the rules of closure overhauled, sharpened, made more applicable, and used. Closure should not be a dirty word, but when the government uses it, it has to be right. It has to be certain that it is on the right issue, and then ultimately the people will decide.
Summer Recess
Having said that, I would not agree to that unless as a corollary there is the opportunity for members of this House to have restored to them many of the rights which have been pilfered and stolen by the government over the course of the last few years.
We are all private members here, except those who are in the cabinet. The members on the government side have the same responsibility as we do for ensuring that the issues of the day are debated, discussed, and brought to a vote, and I think the reason for the way we have been operating in the past-and this is one of the reasons for the frustration and the anxiety which compelled and drove members of the opposition parties to debate Bill C-66 at length as they did-was the fact that we have had no other remedy. That is the only weapon which is left to hon. members sitting in opposition to the government, and even to hon. members on the government side. In this regard I would like to see them recognized with regard to changes which will permit, encourage, and in fact even demand that members on the government side have an opportunity to bring up issues, compel the government to debate those issues, and compel the House to decide and take a vote on them.
Government members say, and this is the standard rhetoric, that they make their influence felt in caucus and the government listens to them. I have been on both sides of the House, and I know how much garbage that kind of statement is. It is a claim to which a minimum amount of credence can be attached.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Our caucus is different.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: You are in the wrong caucus.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
The President of the Privy Council (Mr. Sharp) says his caucus is different. I know it is disciplined and can be brought to heel much more readily, and that the whip is used more frequently.
The case of the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Reid) is before the committee, and I cannot comment. I am not a prophet nor the son of a prophet, but I would like to venture a considerable amount that the committtee will decide, among other things, that the parliamentary secretary had great presence and great perceptiveness; that his crystal ball was beautifully polished; that he could examine that crystal ball; listen to the debate and with marvellous anticipation come up with the legislation, and the budget bill were going to be; and that the amendments to the Income Tax Act, and the budget bill were going to be; and that he operated on that basis and not only discharged his duty but is entitled to be decorated for what he did.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Just like one of your members.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
That is the kind of decision which will come out of that committee, and so I reject all suggestions that members on the government side have any more influence in decision making than we do. In fact I sometimes wonder how much influence the government itself has. To a very great extent the members of the cabinet are only the surrogates of the senior civil servants who, speaking figuratively, allow them to come in here and announce decisions which the civil service has brought into effect.

July 30, 1975
Summer Recess
There are a great many people who at one time graced the civil service who know this to be a fact. I am looking at one right now, and I know that he would like to agree with me, although he may not say so.
What we must have here for all parties on all sides of the House is the right at certain times to bring up for discussion, debate, and decision, issues which are current, controversial, and which need to be aired.
This country gives place of residence to many people, and a great many pluralistic groups live here. Their views should be reflected by an opportunity to have votes. I hope my colleague, the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath), will have something to say later on about fishermen. I encourage him to make a speech with regard to their problems, but that is the kind of issue where there should be an opportunity for a two or three hour debate with a certainty that there will be a vote. That is a matter of working things out between the House leaders of all parties so that this may be done.
By the facts of life enough time must be allowed for the government to pursue its own policies, but if what I propose is done then the people of the country will know that vicariously through their representatives in this House their points of view are in fact being put forward, being considered, and even though they may not be accepted, at least they are getting their day in court. If that is not done, I do not really give this parliament too much hope of continuing in a meaningful way. Although I am not one of those who says parliament will vanish, its effectiveness, its usefulness, its capacity to do things for the people of this country, which is now greatly impaired, will suffer to such an extent that the present indifference of people to parliament and its institutions will be heightened. People will dismiss us as being of no use.
I suggest to members of the government that as they exist now-in between elections with a majority-they can become fat, sluggish, and complacent. They know they are going to get their money under the appropriations bill, that the estimates are bound to be deemed to be passed as of a certain date, that they can bring in controversial bills at the tag end of the session and, by a process of exhaustion, as with Bill C-66, the legislation will be passed.
I am looking at the Postmaster General (Mr. Mackasey) who, I am sure, agrees with me. He has been an effective debater both in opposition and in government. He knows the necessity of restoring to this House the cut and thrust of debate on current and controversial issues which need to be ventilated to show the people that we are a force to be reckoned with.
In the limited time available to us this fall there will not be too much opportunity to make changes in the rules of the House. I suggest through you, Madam Speaker, through the government, and through all members, that we must bring ourselves to some form of agreement to have these sorts of debates, coupled with an opportunity to allow the government to use closure from time to time to speed up the process.
I do not suggest agreement in advance as to allocation of time. I would resist strenuously any suggestion that if the government says it wants 60 bills passed we should agree

to devote three hours to one or three hours to another. Not until a bill has been debated on second reading and/or in committee should there by any discussion as to the length of time fixed for debate. I think we are reasonable enough people, however, that if there is opportunity for the kind of debate we ought to have, enough people would agree to a reasonable limit.
Private members have a duty to perform. They represent the people of Canada with all their warts, virtues, and defects. Only by the process of meaningful reasonable debate in this House can we achieve the objective we were sent here to attain.

Madam Speaker, the motion we are debating today is a motion to adjourn the longest continuous sitting of this House in 11 years. I wish that those of us who are going to take part in the debate could conclude that it has been a productive session that brought about real benefits for the people of Canada; unfortunately the opposite conclusion would have to be reached by anyone looking at the record.
In virtually every crucial area of public concern the government has shown its lack of direction. It has either had no policy or, where policy has been indicated in a general way, it has totally lacked detailed implementation. It has failed in the most fundamental way to live up to the mandate it was given in the election of 1974.
In that victory the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) for the first time gained the support of a substantial number of average and low income Canadians on the basis of a specific program. In 1968 he went to the country as a smiling Mackenzie King who liked to dance. At that time in Canadian history he had a personality appeal. We were over the puritan stage and Canadians thought it was appropriate then for a politician to show that he enjoyed life. With this revelation the Prime Minister managed to get a lot of people to support him on the rather unsubstantial basis that a man who enjoyed life could not be all wrong. It turned out between 1968 and 1972 that he was almost all wrong.
He went into the election in 1972 not as a swinging and smiling Mackenzie King but as a retired philosopher from some university department. Yes, as an hon. member suggests, a good third year student assessing his philosophical debates with Canadians in 1972 would have concluded that they were even rubbishy as philosophy. He did not go to the people of Canada on such practical matters which he regarded as mundane, as housing, the cost of living, unemployment, and regional disparity. He used the slogan "The land is strong"; he wanted to have a dialogue with the people in 1972. The people showed him what they thought of his performance from 1968 to 1972, and what they thought of the kind of campaign that he conducted in 1972. The Liberals almost got booted out of office; they hung on only by the skin of their teeth.
In 1974, and I say this in all seriousness, the Prime Minister looked on the average person's concern for the first time in a campaign. We were on his side when he rejected the wage and price freeze policy of the Conservative Party. But I am not going to debate the merits of that now. The point is that the Prime Minister took an unequivocal position on that and told fishermen on the
July 30, 1975

east coast, workers in the industrial cities, and farmers on the prairies, "We reject that policy because we want to do something for the average Canadian". He did not bother with them in 1968 or 1972, but he did in 1974.
Before the election in 1974 he said in Vancouver, "Housing is in a state of crisis" for the average and low income Canadian, and promised that the Liberals would do something about it. He also said the Liberals would do something about Canadian ownership of natural resources, and promised that at last 50 per cent of new investment in the resource sector would be Canadian.
He then got into transportation policy and said that in terms of interurban transportation Canadian cities were in a mess-after about 20 years of Liberal government. He talked about transportation needs as a continental problem, and of redressing the legitimate grievances of the Atlantic provinces and the prairies in regard to the freight rate system. He spoke directly to the ordinary people of Canada and said, "If you elect the Liberal Party we will do something about the transportation system".
Just name the issue, Madam Speaker, and we can document from the Prime Minister's campaign speeches in 1974 the specific commitments he made. I have listed some of the major ones-housing, transportation, foreign ownership and, related to that, job creation and so on, in a Canadian owned economy. Then, preeminently came the question of inflation and unemployment. He said that the Liberals would really do something for ordinary Canadians. It is a record that we now have to assess. He made no such promise in 1968; he just went on the superficial image that he and his party had professionally packaged. In 1972 he attempted to philosophize. In 1974 he came on as addressing himself to the concerns of ordinary people. It is to his record in this field we have to address ourselves, and it is with this in mind we must assess the work of the present session.
What has it done, that marvelous party which promised to improved conditions for the average Canadian? I will tell you, Madam Speaker. This has probably been the most reactionary government we have seen since the Second World War. Indeed, it is probably the most reactionary government of any country in the western world.
I invite the smirking and smiling Liberal backbenchers across the way to assess with some degree of dispassionate honesty the record of the government which was elected to meet the needs of ordinary Canadians. Who has profited from its incomes policy? Has there been a redistribution of income in favour of the poor, in favour of those with average incomes? Who has benefitted from the economic independence program? Has any move been made in this field? Who has benefitted from the housing program? These questions are the real test.
What has the government done in the broad constitutional sphere of federal-provincial relations? Under the Prime Minister we have seen the introduction of the worst set of policies since the Second World War. Unilateral and arbitrary measures have been imposed infringing upon provincial areas of responsibility and undermining the relationship between the federal government and the provinces to an extent not previously known, at least in
Summer Recess
the past decade. I hear an hon. member asking me to be specific. I will oblige him. I refer, first of all, to what appeared in last year's budget-the resource policy of the federal government which was opposed by every province in Canada.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Not true. It was not opposed in every province.

Then there was the budget of most recent date which undermined the national standard of medicare and hospitalization which had been established in recent decades. Again the government took on virtually every province in the country, except the wealthiest-they are interested, perhaps, in taking over the financing of health and medicare programs provided, of course, that the federal government agrees to transfer some taxation points. As I say, only the wealthiest provinces are interested because they stand to gain. But every poor province in Canada-and that means many poor Canadians-will suffer because of the position the federal government has taken.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Not true.
There is the disruption of medicare, unilaterally imposed, that disruption of national standards by the government opposite-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: There are poor Canadians in Oshawa.

The hon. member says I live in Oshawa. Of course I live in Oshawa, and Oshawa happens to be in Ontario which is a wealthy province. But I, as a member of a socialist party, am concerned about the province from which the hon. member who interrupted me comes, a province which is a lot less wealthy.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The hon. member did not understand my interjection. I said he should not make the mistaken relationship of calling people in poor provinces poor people. I just don't like that.

I did not realize the hon. member was so sensitive. I do not believe it does a service to a poor Canadian to say he is not a poor Canadian. The party of which I am a member is interested in dealing with that problem and changing the situation, whereas the government which the hon. member supports is a government which will increase poverty in the province from which he comes.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: If hon. members on the government side of the House wish to participate in the debate they will be given an opportunity.
Hear, hear!

I should like to move on now from the marvelous job the government has done in terms of federal-provincial relationships and consider what this means in terms of increasing regional disparities within the country as opposed to decreasing them. In particular I should like to deal with the economic policies emanating from the government since we were called into session last fall.

July 30, 1975
Summer Recess
Two budgets have been produced, one last fall and one just a month ago. What did these two budgets accomplish? Did they have the effect of reducing inequalities? No. The reverse was the case. In the budget of last fall further tax concessions were made for the benefit of the corporate sector. This amounted to a redistribution of income, taking income from the ordinary Canadian and adding it to the corporate sector. Further, special tax concessions were allowed to upper income Canadians who wished to invest in the apartment construction business. This was all very well for people with disposable income for investment. They would gain advantage both ways; they would own the building later on and, in the meantime, they could collect rent, and the money they invested was taken right off the top of their taxable income.
As I say, the budget of last fall did nothing to reduce inequalities in Canada. On the contrary, it increased them. The budget which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) brought down over a month ago, did exactly the same. I have already mentioned the regressive step taken in the field of medicare and hospitalization. As hon. members are aware, the excise tax was discussed at some length in the debate which has quite properly occupied us for some weeks. This, as many of us have pointed out, is another regressive measure. But I would draw attention now to yet another regressive measure having to do with the funding of the unemployment insurance fund.
Instead of maintaining the principle that the people of Canada, through general revenue, should be responsible for the unemployment insurance fund since it is the government which is ultimately responsible for unemployment, where the level exceeds 3 per cent or 4 per cent, the government having, ultimately, control over monetary and fiscal policy, we find that a new floor level has now been introduced-the level at which the taxpayer will begin to make contributions. Coincidentally, of course, this means no call will be made on general revenue until unemployment reaches certain levels. This year it would have been 5.3 per cent; next year it will be in the region of 6 per cent, and the year after that it may be in the region of 7 per cent.
This means that the average man or woman working in Canada faces a substantial increase in premiums to finance the unemployment insurance scheme. Instead of funds coming out of general revenue which is based on income tax, a relatively progressive tax, and corporation taxes, workers will be called upon to finance their own provision for unemployment although the government, and therefore the community as a whole, should be held generally responsible.
In the resource field the Prime Minister promised that the government would do something about increasing Canadian ownership. In one of his election speeches he declared that 50 per cent Canadian ownership would be mandatory for all new investment in the resource sector. That is great talk at election time. A lot of us, though, were cynical about the depth of the Liberal commitment to following it up, and as soon as we say the implementation of phase II of the Foreign Investment Review Act we found that the greatest justification for our skepticism. It became abundantly clear when phase II was revealed that the government not only was not concerned about dealing

with the existing problem of foreign ownership in Canada, but was also unconcerned about controlling new foreign investment in this country.
The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie) in one of his more candid admissions before the television cameras acknowledged that he did not expect any real decline in foreign investment in the economy. What an admission from a cabinet minister in a party that just a year ago made a commitment to the people of Canada that it would do something serious about the problems of foreign ownership!
What about housing? A crisis was described by the Prime Minister three or four days before the election last year. The crisis has gotten worse since that time, not better. If you look at the housing starts in January, February, March and April of this year, you see that every month there was a substantial decline compared to the year before. With the election of the Liberals last July, the party that said they would do something about housing, rather than the crisis being mitigated, it has been exacerbated. The housing problem has gotten worse, not better.
Not because of the Liberals.
Who else is governing? Is it the Conservative Party that is governing?
Look at the record.
It is the Liberal Party that is governing, but they are not responsible?
That is not what I said.

All that we have had with regard to housing is a repetition of the policies that failed before the 1974 election. Before that election we had a bald headed minister responsible for housing. The Prime Minister changed that. Now we have a minister with some hair. Maybe the Prime Minister was acting on the assumption that a little hair means a little brains and that that would result in a change in policy. However, we did not get that. We got a minister from Toronto who is duplicating every error made by the previous minister from Vancouver. Instead of improving, the housing situation has become worse.
We then come to transportation. That is a real gem. In one of those rare moments of candour and insight shown by a cabinet minister, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) said that transportation policy is in a mess. That is what he said prior to the 1974 election campaign. It is now over a year later, and transportation policy is still in a mess.
When members of the Conservative, NDP, and Social Credit parties asked the minister what he was going to do about freight rates, the failure in providing boxcars, and the needs of the people in our cities in terms of an urban transit system, the minister kept saying that the policy was in a mess. We had to agree. He repeatedly asked us to have a little patience as the government would be presenting a grand policy. We waited and waited. Finally we got a general statement of policy. The guidelines that were in
July 30, 1975

the policy we waited for were absurd and contradictory. I will not go into great detail. We got another statement which was equivalent to the election platitudes that we got prior to the election of last July. Not one bill of substance with regard to a transportation policy has been brought before this House since the election.
I have referred to the problems with regard to housing, foreign ownership, and transportation. I do not intend to be too much longer. I am sure the Liberals will not be disappointed to hear that. Before saying something about the general economic policy, however, I cannot ignore two other issues which have been of concern to Canadians and this parliament, and which the government has not dealt with in an adequate way.
The first is the use to be made of the Canadian development of nuclear technology. I refer to the CANDU project. If there has been a solid and persistent bungling of an issue, it has been the government's policy with regard to CANDU. The government is still committed to selling nuclear reactors to Argentina and South Korea, two of the most unstable and reactionary governments in the world.
I could elaborate with respect to members of the Conservative Party who followed that issue-and I give them credit-with immense care, as well as certain of my colleagues, notably the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas), and the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin). I could document in two hours of speeches the bungling and contradictory nature of the government's CANDU policy which will result in our providing the capacity to develop nuclear weapons to the governments of Argentina and South Korea. Surely that is an act of self-condemnation about which it is hard to say anything more.
There is another issue which is of concern to fishermen on the east coast, those from Newfoundland in particular, as well as those on the west coast. I refer to the jurisdictional authority that we are prepared to assume over our coastal waters. We believe in negotiation, but this has been going on for so many years that it is well beyond the time for talk. Our party has argued that the government should unilaterally assert jurisdictional authority over our coastal waters up to 200 miles, or to the continental shelf, whichever is farther. Unless the government begins quickly to move in that direction, and it may be too late already, we are going to lose the invaluable fishing stock off our two coasts, particularly the east coast. Again the government vacillates, does not act, and promises further conferences.
Whether we are talking about housing, transportation policies, Canadian ownership of our resources, fishermen on our east or west coasts or, sensible world-wide use of technology developed in Canada in a nuclear age, the government has been a colossal failure in its first year in office.
I want to conclude my remarks by saying something about the very serious state of the Canadian economy and the equally serious failure of the government to deal with the situation. In July of last year the government was given a mandate on the economic issue above all others, if we are to single out one matter. It took the position that it, and it alone, could deal with the twin problems of inflation and unemployment. If a survey were taken of Canadi-
Summer Recess
ans from coast to coast asking on what issue they voted in the government, my guess is that it would be that twin issue they cited most often.
Let us consider this policy matter and test the government to see whether it has lived up to its mandate, namely, general economic policy. How well has it done in the year since it was elected? In June, 1974, there was 4.9 per cent of the labour force unemployed. One year later, after the leadership and the dynamic policy innovations of the Liberal government, did unemployment drop below the 4.9 level of 1974? No, Mr. Speaker; it rose to 7.2 per cent. Unemployment went up after the election of this majority government, not down.
In actual numbers, which are more meaningful in terms of real life experience, unemployment moved from 465,000 in June, 1974, to 725,000. This number comprises men and women, young and old, in every part of the country. In other words, after one year of this government there was an increase of some 260,000 Canadians on the unemployment rolls.
If we look at the inflation picture the situation is just as dismal and the failure of the government just as great. In June, 1974, the consumer price index stood at 166.7. By June of this year it was 184. As a percentage this works out to 10.4 per cent higher than it was a year ago.
So much for the Liberal's success in coping with inflation. The figures I have just given do not, of course, include the ten cents a gallon excise tax. Nor do they include the effects of the $1.50 a barrel increase in the price of crude oil which the government introduced in the last budget, or the increase in the price of natural gas. All of these added together-and I say this with care-it has been calculated by some responsible experts in and out of political parties, will probably add another 2 per cent or 3 per cent to the cost of living figures in the coming months. In other words, the government has been a failure in dealing with the major issue on which it was elected in the 1974 campaign, namely, the twin problems of inflation and unemployment.
What about the future general economic picture, Mr. Speaker? Unfortunately, the record of increasing unemployment and inflation since June of 1974 is not going to level out and remain constant; it is going to increase in both dimensions. Let me refer my Liberal colleagues opposite to the results of a recent study put out by Wood Gundy, hardly a noted socialist company. I ask the members of the government to consider their forecast. They say that for this year inflation and unemployment will both get worse. They forecast a rate of some 8 per cent unemployment for the end of this year. That, I suggest, is a conservative estimate; certainly it is from a conservative source. So the trend is an unhealthy one, one that is not good for Canadians.
Rather than introducing programs to reduce unemployment, the most recent budget, for reasons that I indicated at the time and which I will not repeat now, and which other commentators advanced, will increase unemployment. The forecast of Wood Gundy regarding inflation is just as negative. In June the consumer price index stood, as I said, at 184. They forecast that by the end of this year

July 30, 1975
Summer Recess
it will go up about another five points, surely an undesirable situation.
I will conclude on that pessimistic note. We have ended the longest continuous part of a session since 1964. I think all members on both sides of the House have worked hard in terms of their individual contributions. But let me repeat what I said at the outset. In view of the commitment of the Prime Minister and his government in July of 1974 to the average and working people of Canada, one he did not make in 1972 or 1968, in terms of our legislative output here, this last year must be considered to be a very substantial failure, one that affects in a negative way the real life experience of average and low income Canadians from coast to coast. It is this kind of experience that I hope the government will reflect upon, so that when we come back in the fall we can begin to do something of substance, not of rhetoric, in terms of meeting the housing needs, the transportation needs, and the economic independence needs of the people of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I merely wish to make a few points concerning the adjournment motion and take this opportunity to say how ridiculous is the situation on this 30th of July as I rise to speak. This is to remind hon. members of the House that for years we have been urging Parliament and the government to alter the regulations in this connection, in order to have a more serious framework than at the present time. When fully conscious adults who represent the elite of the country are having a good time engaged in a war of attrition to pass a legislation, Mr. Speaker, I think it lacks seriousness.
Who is to blame? The opposition? The government? Of course the government members say: "Well, it is your fault, you should end the debate." And we say: "Well it is your fault, you should withdraw that bill." And so we manage to sit till July 30. I was first elected in 1968, that is seven years ago. I think this is the third time we have been sitting so late in the summer.
And yet, Mr. Speaker, this problem could be solved quite easily. Why not simply set opening and closing dates? It would be so simple to say that the session will open on the second Monday of September and close on the Friday preceeding June 24. Then, it would be possible to plan and co-ordinate our parliamentary work. This, of course, would make it mandatory for the government to arrange its legislative program in a better fashion. And within the set dates we would really accomplish the work the government has deemed should be completed during the year, or session.
The government could then easily solve all kinds of small problems by advising us in advance of its intentions. For instance, we could obtain during the intersession a copy of the proposed bills; the order in which they would be debated could also be given. Consequently, we would have more time for ourselves as representatives to consider these bills, do our research and therefore, introduce in this House more concrete, more specific suggestions.
I think that could be done easily, and we would then be looked upon as people who are a little more serious and

know what they have to do and do their job in a very conscientious way. I shall not linger over all the inconveniences of being in the dark about the opening and closing dates of a session but may I be permitted nevertheless, Mr. Speaker, to say that impossibility to know when we are going to start and when we are going to finish disturbs the family life of everyone of us, prevents us from planning our work during the intersession and consequently results in inconveniences that could be avoided pretty easily. That is why I take the opportunity of this debate on the motion to adjourn to advise the government to come up with a change of rules in that respect.
I would also like to echo the two hon. members who spoke before me and make a few remarks about the business that was submitted to us for consideration during this session. Of course, I will be told that it is easy for a member of the opposition to criticize, that is his role, he must do it and consequently we are talking for nothing. Mr. Speaker, I say that is wrong. I think we are trying to really reflect public opinion and when we opposed even fiercely the last bill which was passed yesterday it was because we knew quite well that people did not want that unwarranted increase in the price of gas with that excise tax.
We saw since the beginning of this session how different it was. We saw once again the tremendous difference there was between a majority government and a minority government. It is all nice to say that a majority government brings with it instability and everything else but a minority government showed, for example, that it was for the people. If Bill C-66 had been introduced in 1972 or 1973, we know quite well that it would not have been passed. That was the advantage of having a minority government which had better chances of being on the taxpayer's side. We saw during this session that the government, under the present Prime Minister, had returned to its attitude of complacency, not to say of arrogance, to simply impose things that nobody wants and forget others that should not be forgotten.
For example, the legislation that we were eager to have before us was the old age security legislation, since during the last electoral campaign, politicians were travelling around, and especially in Quebec, voicing the slogan "Old age pension at 60". We were thus expecting, after all the representations and the efforts which had been made, particularly by the members of the party I represent, that they would bring in a piece of legislation on old age security which would be truly adequate and would meet the needs of the population.
What was introduced, Mr. Speaker? One must admit there is a small improvement, but it is so slight that one can barely speak of an improvement since our suggestions were not even included in the bill. First of all, pensionable age should have been lowered to 60: that would have solved the problem. Secondly, it was to be granted merely to the spouses of those aged 65 who needed it. We agree with that, but then we noticed, which we pointed out to the House, that the case had been overlooked where the person dies. That is normal, natural: it happens. Whoever suddenly becomes a widower or a widow, no matter, will lose the pension. That seems obvious.
July 30, 1975

Let us take the case of a lady of 62 whose husband is 70; she would be entitled to the pension and the income supplement, because they have no other income. Consequently, they would get some $400 a month but because her husband is going to die and the wife will be only 62, she will lose what she was entitled to. It is nonsense. I think that, when something as simple, as obvious as that is underlined, the Minister of National Health and Welfare should understand it and amend the act accordingly. We are going to run into huge difficulties. As my hon. colleague from Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert) said, what is going to happen? That 62 year old widow will still have to rely on the welfare benefits to eke out a living, whereas everything could be solved easily. But maybe she will solve her case in a way that is almost suggested in that bill by simply shacking up, as they say. Then she will be entitled to her pension.
It would be so easy to correct all that. Of course, they will always say that inflation should be avoided these days, and therefore, expenses have to be cut down, not increased. Mr. Speaker, we have never accepted that argument and we shall never accept it, for if the slightest attention were paid to the solutions we are suggesting on the economic and financial points of view, we are sure that we would really be fighting inflation. But as long as we have no true solutions, no basic solutions, we shall be plagued with the cancer of inflation, we shall be left with a government that will indulge in stop-gap, temporary solutions, whereas the basic problem is a crucial one.
But the government will simply answer us that if unem-ployemnt keeps rising, if inflation goes on spiralling, if prices keep soaring, there is nothing they can do because it is a world-wide phenomenon. We have heard that for months, especially during the electoral campaign last year, and we still hear it.
Mr. Speaker, as I said, I shall never believe that we in Canada are not able to produce everything we need. And if it were only a matter of money, let us release the funds we need to assist production and meet the needs of all Canadian citizens. It is a basic principle, which should not be questioned. And no one could seriously answer: "Well, it is not our fault, the fault lies with the United States and Europe".
We are now faced with surpluses of powdered milk. Milk producers are being told that they will have to pay 45 per cent more a hundred weight because we have to keep up prices on account of the European Common Market. There again, Mr. Speaker, I say that it is a question of bad reasoning and bad judgment, because absolutely nothing should prevent Canadian dairy farmers from producing milk at a cost that would actually result in reasonable profits and that would at the same time be favourable to all consumers. And if we tried to arrive at a certain equation or balance between consumption and production, such problems would be nonexistent.
But when our government still keeps our doors wide open to commodities we can readily produce ourselves in surplus quantities, I say that if the government pursues such a course of action, nothing will be resolved. Millions of pounds of cheese are entering Canada, whereas are own cheese producers are penalized because they overproduce.
Summer Recess
It's absolutely illogical. Why continue to hang on to such policies when everyone knows they are bad?
That being so, Mr. Speaker, I say we must stop producing and start importing every commodity that costs less than what we produce here. That being so, we will sit down, relax and wait for others to come and feed, dress and house us. That is bad reasoning. The only solution is that if we have the potential and the capacity to produce here what we need, we just have to make it financially possible. Is it as simple as that. And never will I be led to believe anything else.
But it is not so. Policies should be geared to that. The problem will never be solved by waiting for the good "contribution" of the United States, by waiting for milk and butter from New Zealand and Australia and for textile from Japan and Korea. We will never solve our real economic problems by relying on foreign countries. We must not interfere in their internal affairs, and consequently we do not even know whether the competition they offer with their products is real. Whether it is true that they produce cheaper, we do not know. We do not control those countries.
Therefore the government measures should aim at promoting domestic production, which would have the happy effect, Mr. Speaker, of solving our unemployment problem.
What are we doing about manufactures or textiles plants closing down in Quebec when we see ships full of textiles from other countries unloading here? Then we put $4 billion in the unemployment insurance fund to pay those who do not work because government policies prevent them from doing so. If we do not produce everything we need, of course we will have unemployment; it is simple, Mr. Speaker, and I do not understand why we fail to see that.
Of course, this is why we are forced to do negatively the work of the government during this session, since nothing has been proposed to solve the very serious problem we are facing, inflation. Absolutely nothing.
To conclude, there is another point I would like to make. This government does not really try to reach a practical understanding with the provinces. There is now a constitutional problem in Canada. Closing our eyes to the problem will not solve it. The problem is there. There is a current example in the field of communications, with contradictory positions taken by Quebec and the Canadian government.
What does the government do about it? It plays the strong man. It digs in and says: "We are right, that is the end of it, go back to your places." That, Mr. Speaker, is an excellent way of inviting trouble. Instead, the government should ask itself what do Quebecers want. If Quebecers answer they want control over communications, let them have it. That is true democracy. We have no authority to judge. As I indicated to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) himself, there are times when we must go above the constitution and say: That is that. Mr. Speaker, it is only by chance that the federal government entered the communications field. It is only because the provinces did not move in in the first place. It is simply because an act of the Quebec Legislative Assembly, now the National Assembly,

July 30, 1975
The Royal Assent
was never implemented that control over radio, television and communications in general is now in federal hands. If the provinces had wanted to take it, they would have done so. It is not because an error was committed there at other times that the views of provinces should still be denied.
For that reason, I believe the federal government's attitude in this area would have serious if not disastrous consequences. I must once more blame the government for its attitude in this area. If we are going to have a truly united Canada, it is essential that the provinces be given a fair hearing. It is also essential that we get truly interested in Canada's various regions and their needs. That is important, that is essential. We must not try and solve problems simply by stating they do not exist. In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I will make only one wish, namely that the next session give us the opportunity to debate bills which are really concrete and aim at helping the Canadian people. I shall then be pleased to give credit to the government for it.
