Mr. Speaker, it is not a point of order, but I would like to take part in the debate. I do not intend to speak at length because I do not want to prolong the debate. What I want to do, Mr. Speaker, is to draw the attention of hon. members and, particularly, of the government on the tragic disaster which happened in the Iles-de-la-Madeleine, in my riding, when Hurricane Blanche swept through the area the day before yesterday, July 28.
Even if the damages are not as heavy as at Saint-Bona-venture, the losses suffered by the islanders represent a great trial and will deprive most of them of their means of living for a long time. Hurricane Blanche tore off and blew over the roofs of motels and houses, lit fires which destroyed herring smoke houses in Cap-aux-Meules and many houses, sank many fishing boats and other boats, damaged many others, caused untold damages at the harbour of Millerand, which is being upgraded. One person, Miss Jocelyne LeBlanc, died in a fire during that tragedy. The current assessment of damages which have been reported to me this morning lies between $3.5 million to $4 million. I take this opportunity to extend my condolences to Mr. and Mrs. Fortune LeBlanc, the parents of Jocelyne and to all the members of their family, following the death of their daughter in the fire which also destroyed their home.
I also wish to express my sincere condolences to the people of Iles-de-la-Madeleine tried by this tragic disaster and I want to assure them of my entire cooperation in this sad event. I urge the Canadian government to bring all the help they can give in the circumstances to these people, so that they might recover as soon as possible from this sudden disaster, without unduly mortgaging their future.

July 30, 1975

Mr. Speaker, I would like to involve myself in this debate for just a few moments, and I would like to associate myself with the remarks which were just made by the hon. member for Bonaventure-Iles-de-la-Madeleine (Mr. Bechard), as well as with the hon. member for Drummond (Mr. Pinard) with regard to the tragic circumstances in recent days in the Drummond constituency where, at St. Bonaventure, a tornado struck, taking the lives and injuring a number of people there, and couple that with the tragic circumstances associated with the town of Spring-hill in my constituency, which fortunately did not involve the loss of any lives, as was the case in the two previous disasters, but did destroy the whole business section of the town of Springhill and, as a result, added a tragedy on top of a number of recent tragedies that have occurred over the last two decades in that community, as many Canadians are aware.
Some members of the House might not be aware of what has happened in Springhill. In 1956 we had a coal mine disaster that took the lives of 39 miners. In 1957 we had a very severe fire that destroyed a good part of the business district of the town, and which was later rebuilt. In 1958 we had another coal mine disaster which took the lives of 79 miners, eliminated the only real industry left in that community and the coal mining operations that were there.
Because of subsequent government actions, both federal and provincial, we were able to rebuild the town of Springhill and give it a new economic base. One of the major contributions towards that was the establishment of two penitentiaries in that community, which gave economic viability and confidence to the business community, allowing them to reinvest in the town and rebuild.
In recent days we have had three very serious and tragic disasters that struck Springhill and two different communities in Quebec. I must say that while this is usually the time to criticize the government and to point out what it has not done, I want to say first of all that I personally appreciated the attitude of all members of the House with regard to the problems that are associated with the Springhill tragedy, and I want to say as well that I have been impressed by the hon. member for Drummond who immediately rose in the House and brought to the attention of the government and the House the tragic event that took place in St. Bonaventure, just as the hon. member for Bonaventure-iles-de-la-Madeleine did this afternoon with regard to his constituency.
I was pleased as well to see that the hon. member for Saint Hyacinthe (Mr. Wagner) also rose in the House and indicated the support of all members in our party in connection with the tragic circumstances associated with the tragedy in Drummond. Today the hon. member for Frontenac-Lennox and Addington (Mr. Alkenbrack) indicated some concern over the fact that maybe sufficient attention was not being given to the circumstances surrounding the tragedy at Drummond, and indicated his hope that the governments, both federal and provincial, will do anything they can to assist those people and help them to rebuild the town and the homes that were destroyed by the tornado.
Summer Recess
There are times when the public or members, regardless of party, find fault with the government. But in so far as the tragedy at Springhill is concerned, I must say that the government and the ministers who are particularly involved deserve a good deal of credit for the way in which they banded together to try to find what they could do at the federal level to assist in rebuilding the community there.
I think that special credit should be given to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Jamieson), who acted as liaison between the various cabinet ministers in trying to assist by putting together a group of proposals from the federal government without its having had any specific request from the province of Nova Scotia, trying to use federal programs to restore confidence in the people of Springhill by showing that there are others in this country who are concerned and aware of their problems. This will assist them in setting the town back on the road to recovery, and in giving it an economic base which will make it a viable community once more.
I mentioned the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion, and I certainly must also mention the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand), with whom I often cannot agree. Nor can I always support the policies he purports to stand for in association with his department, but certainly in so far as he was concerned about Springhill and the possibility of locating another penal institution there, his reaction was immediate, and the activities of his department are obvious to the people in that community today.
There is work being done to ascertain whether a new, smaller institution could be established there which would provide additional employment, and additional confidence in the minds of the business community, which would be of material assistance in giving an economic base to those people who must be having difficulty deciding whether to rebuild or to put the insurance cheques in their pockets.
I must also say that the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras) reacted in a very commendable way by saying that because of the problems that community faces, and because of the very great havoc which has been created by the fire, he is willing to eliminate the possibility of delay in starting new LIP projects, allowing them to move forward quicker so that the town can be cleaned up and look presentable, so that when people come there they may give favourable consideration to undertaking whatever they intend to undertake.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I certainly will not hold proceedings up very much longer at this point. I did want to point out, however, ways and means by which the federal government can participate and be of assistance in a constituency struck by disaster, without the provincial government having to make application under the disaster relief formula. This formula makes it very difficult for a provincial government to seek support at the federal level because of the heavy involvement that might be useful when a disaster is province-wide and involves expenditure of millions of dollars. In specific areas the formula does not work. The federal and provincial governments have to work together to try to overcome the disabilities faced by the stricken communities.
Some people may be concerned about the constituency of Drummond and the fact that the government of Quebec does not wish to apply to the federal government for disaster relief under the federal-provincial formula. At the same time there are ways in which the federal and provin-
July 30, 1975

cial governments can work together. I believe they are doing so very effectively in Nova Scotia now to overcome the disabilities which face the community of Springhill.
I have mentioned a number of programs, but to be fair to the other ministers involved I think I should mention them also. The Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Jamieson) is looking into the possibility of setting up a textile industry in the community. He has expressed his willingness, too, to involve himself in efforts by the provincial government to establish an industrial park in that area to help attract the new industries which are needed. Moreover, he has indicated to me that the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Danson) is undertaking certain plans in cooperation with the government of Nova Scotia to provide housing for people who have lost their homes as a result of the fire.
These programs, which are in addition to those I mentioned earlier, will go a long way toward restoring confidence among the inhabitants and giving an incentive to the people in the Springhill area to take this tragedy in their stride and build a new town.
Another idea has been mentioned to me-in fact, it came from Senator Graham from Nova Scotia. So complete was the destruction caused by the fire that an opportunity presents itself to build a completely new downtown district, an endeavour in which the federal government might be able to involve itself through various programs already under way. Ideas of this sort emanate not only from all quarters of this House but, as I have mentioned, from members of the other place, even though the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) believes that very little emanates from there that is of any value to anyone.
Well said.

To the other two hon. members who have experienced the same kind of tragic situation associated with disasters, I would say there are many ways in which they could work with the federal government and provincial governments to see that their communities are brought back to viable economic life.
The other point I wish to bring up concerns a responsibility of the CRTC. It relates to television coverage in my constituency. My constituency happens to border on New Brunswick, and everything we get on television comes from either New Brunswick or Prince Edward Island. There is nothing from Nova Scotia. We are almost led to believe we are in a different province when we turn on our television sets because nothing associated with Nova Scotia ever gets to us.
I have brought up this subject previously. I have appeared before the CRTC and I have made representations concerning it, but I have never been able to get any satisfaction. Along with this, we have a cablevision operator in the town of Truro who operates a cablevision service for both Truro and Bible Hill. He insists on giving the people of that area nothing that they ought not to be able to get without cablevision. In other words, they can only get two television stations which they should, in any case, be able to get without cablevision. However, because of "holes" in reception, the only way people can get a good picture is by purchasing cable. The cablevision operator
Summer Recess
will not provide any of the inducements offered by other cablevision operators in Nova Scotia. Incidentally, I notice that the CRTC recently allowed him to increase his rates.
I have had the CRTC carry out a special investigation into this matter. They gave me a report which, as far as I am concerned, was just a whitewash. Something should be done to see that this cablevision operator either produces an inducement for people to pay special rates at least equivalent to those provided, for example, by the cablevision operation in Amherst-the channels in the area plus two American channels-or that somebody else takes over the operation in the Truro-Bible Hill area.
I wish to thank hon. members for their patience in listening to these remarks, and to thank you, Mr. Speaker, and to wish you a very enjoyable recess.

First of all, Mr. Speaker, I suppose I should apologise to hon. members for detaining them at this late hour close to the adjournment of the session. However, I regret I cannot extend such an apology because the matter I have to raise is one of such serious consequence that I would not be doing my duty if I did not bring it before the chamber this afternoon.
Earlier today, under Standing Order 43,1 sought leave to move a motion with reference to the serious situation at the Sydney steel plant where 500 workers have been laid off since March. Apparently in the last few days difficulties have arisen in connection with the rail bill and it would appear that we will now see a few hundred more laid off.
The federal government has involved itself with the affairs of the steel plant on several occasions, providing assistance for which we are very grateful, and which was forthcoming despite the fact that this was a Crown corporation operated by the province.
My purpose in seeking to move a motion under Standing Order 43 was that I felt that this was a situation which should be looked into by the federal government. The motion was that, in view of the problem, the government should check with the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, the Department of Labour, and the Department of Manpower and Immigration to get from those departments a team of experts who would go to Sydney immediately in order to determine what assistance could be rendered, either technical or financial.
I had hoped to ask a question, but the question period today was quite busy. This is the reason why I bring it to the attention of the House at this time. I feel the team of experts could do something to assist that operation. All parties in the House agreed to the motion, with the exception of a Liberal member. That was very unfortunate because this is a very serious situation, coming on top of an announcement a few weeks ago that we are going to lose the Toyota assembly plant of Canadian Motor Industries. We will suddenly lose jobs there.
Not too many months ago we lost the General Instruments Corporation plant which assembled electronic devices, automobile turners, and so on. This resulted in 1,000 people losing their jobs. I raised this with the Minis-

July 30, 1975
Summer Recess
ter of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie), but nothing was done. Those people are still out of work.
We also have the coal mine in Cape Breton which, at the moment, is in danger of being sealed off because of a mine gas explosion. Several hundred employees are not working there, with the exception of the draggermen and what we call the bareface miners. They are risking their lives to put this mine back into condition so that work can again commerce. I must commend the Cape Breton Development Corporation and its president, Mr. Tom Kent, for the extreme effort being made to rehabilitate that mine. I also commend the workers, who on occasion worked around the clock with heavy equipment and gas masks and, of course, the bareface miners who are risking their lives.
I want to bring this problem to the attention of the Acting Prime Minister (Mr. Sharp), who should take it upon himself, if for no other reason than out of the goodness of his heart, to bring the problem to the attention of the cabinet and have it put high on the priority list.
I am happy that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mar-chand) is here. He is a former labour leader who knows the problems of the workers involved in steel and many other industries. I hope that both ministers will use their good offices to bring this to the attention of the cabinet. It is funny that no matter how loud I raise my voice, both cabinet ministers do not seem to be listening. They are conversing, I hope about the problem we are confronted with on Cape Breton Island.
Oh, oh!

If the hon. member who made the interjection would like to identify himself, I will take him to Sydney to explain why he opposed my motion this afternoon which probably would have helped the industry. I will be pleased to escort him to the city of Sydney where he can talk to the steel workers, the businessmen, and others involved in the industry.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip's assistant; Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: I did not make the interjection, but I would love to visit there.

Coming from a steel city, the hon. member knows the problems we face. In any event, I will not detain the House any longer. I know it is unfair to the members who are here. They have received an invitation from Mr. Speaker to attend a reception which they justly deserve.
I implore the Acting Prime Minister to ascertain what can be done with the expertise that is available in the three departments I mentioned, and to assure us that in conjunction with other cabinet ministers he will do his utmost to have every possible assistance rendered to the premier of Nova Scotia, who is on the board. This is a Crown corporation operated by the provincial government.
At the same time I ask him to bring to the attention of the cabinet the new steel complex that was promised for
Cape Breton Island prior to July 8, 1974, something over a year ago. I ask him to ascertain whether that is still in the mill, and I do not mean the steel mill, as to future projections. I want him to assure us that when that complex comes about, it will not be built in some other part of the country. The Liberal candidate in my area assured my people that the steel complex proposed as a result of a study by the Department of Regional Economic Expansion would definitely be in the Cape Breton area.
We now hear the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Jamieson) issuing other sounds. I hope and pray that the day does not come when such a complex comes about that it will be located anywhere other than Cape Breton Island where we have expertise and the work force. God knows we have enough unemployment, ranging between 15 per cent and 20 per cent.
In conclusion, we have heard the slogans of the government during campaigns. "The land is strong". "We have the answers" and a great many others. Unfortunately in our area the land is not strong, and we have found that the government does not have the answers.

Mr. Speaker, like some others I had a speech I could make at this time, but I have filed it. Rather, as one of the oldtim-ers around here, I want to start the process of the appropriate greetings for the occasion. On behalf on my party, and we are unanimous, I extend greetings for a very useful and happy break to all members of the House, to the staff, to those at the table, to Your Honour and all those who occupy the chair.
While I am on my feet may I express the hope that when we come back in the fall the government will present to us the kind of legislation that will enable us to do a better job for the rest of the session. But my main purpose in rising now is to extend greetings to one and all.

Mr. Speaker, following the example of my colleague, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), I shall not make a speech. I wanted, for once, a member on this side to have the last say over our good friend, so I simply echo all his good wishes.
